title: The shell, permissions and sudo
part: Part 1 · The box, the way the gurus run it
brief: Most 'Permission denied' tickets are one missing bit on one directory. Find it in one command, and give sudo out by the command, not by the person.
gurus: Evi Nemeth et al., UNIX and Linux System Administration Handbook

exercises.prompt: /srv/app/config.yml is owned by app:app with mode 640. What can a member of the app group (not the app user itself) do with it?
exercises.explain: 6 is rw- for the owner, 4 is r-- for the group, 0 is --- for everyone else. The kernel applies the first class that matches you (owner, then group, then other) and only that one.

exercises.prompt: appuser gets 'Permission denied' opening /srv/app/logs/app.log. The file is appuser:appuser 0644. /srv/app is root:root 0700. Why?
options: appuser needs execute (search) permission on every directory in the path, and /srv/app gives it none
The file must be owned by root
exercises.explain: Opening a path needs x on every directory above it. namei -l prints owner and mode for each component, so the blocking directory jumps out. Check the plain mode bits before you suspect SELinux.

exercises.prompt: Which single command shows owner and mode for every directory on the path to /srv/app/logs/app.log?
exercises.explain: namei comes with util-linux on almost every distribution; -l is long format (owner, group, mode).

exercises.prompt: The deploy user has passwordless root for everything. Give it exactly what a release needs: restart and status of app.service, as root, by full path. Nothing else.
exercises.hint: Use a Cmnd_Alias with full paths (/usr/bin/systemctl restart app.service, ...) and give deploy only that alias, as (root). Check the syntax with visudo -c -f <file>; never install a sudoers file that visudo has not parsed.
exercises.explain: Least privilege in sudo means full paths, exact arguments, a named target user, and visudo before install. A broken file in /etc/sudoers.d can take sudo away from everyone, which is why visudo -c exists.

checks.name: deploy no longer gets every command
restart of app.service allowed, by full path
status of app.service allowed, by full path
no bare command names (sudo matches full paths)
deploy runs them as root only

exercises.prompt: An AI agent proposes `chmod -R 777 /srv/app` to fix that Permission denied. What do you do?
options: Approve it; it is only a lab
Refuse, find the one missing bit with namei -l, and grant exactly that (here: x on /srv/app for appuser or its group)
Run it with sudo so it definitely works
exercises.explain: 777 makes every file writable by every user and process on the box, including whatever exploits the app next. The fix is the smallest change: one directory, one permission, one principal. Part 3's gates enforce the same rule on the agent.
